evidence: The round-0 hunk interpolates `${oneLine(assessment.impact)}` and `${c.message}` straight into a `<summary>` line of a body GitHub renders, and GitHub's sanitizer permits `<details>`/`<summary>`, so a `</summary>` break-out from an upstream commit message is real; cd02a2b adds escapeHtml at the render boundary plus a strict-semver gate on releaseTag.
guidance_note: When a renderer emits markup the platform will render, escape at the render boundary as you write it and enumerate every context the value lands in (HTML text, URL, link text, markdown inline) in that first pass.

evidence: Verified in cd02a2b: runScopeWorker's pre-fix line was `const { summary, findings, usage } = await spawn(...)` returning `{ name, summary, findings, usage }`, so every `r.assessments` was undefined and the whole assessment feature rendered as unassessed - a genuine feature-breaking bug shipped in the original PR.
guidance_note: When threading a new field end-to-end, write the seam test (worker to aggregate) first - unit tests at both ends stay green while the middle drops the field.

evidence: The sibling `findings` aggregation uses a bare `flatMap(r => r.findings)` and readCollectedReview always returns an assessments array, so the `|| []` on only the new field could hide nothing but a contract break; the agent's consistency argument is the correct reading and 8b1d64d removed it.
guidance_note: When adding a record kind alongside an existing one, copy the existing kind's handling exactly - a fallback that only the new field carries is the tell that the shapes diverged.

evidence: First-seen-wins over concurrently-completing workers makes the displayed verdict depend on arrival order, and the agent's own code comment already called the multi-go.mod case the reason dedupeAssessments exists; mirroring dedupeFindings' cautious merge removes the timing dependence rather than papering over it.
guidance_note: When writing a dedup for a new record kind, mirror the existing dedup's conflict rule instead of defaulting to first-seen - arrival order under concurrency is not a merge rule.

evidence: `gh pr diff 95` confirms the pre-PR signature was already 7 positional params and this PR appended `dependencyBumps = []` at position 8, so the reviewer's specific 'insert between 4 and 5' risk is not worsened here; the smell is real, and PR#97 shows buildReviewInput later converted to an options object, so the deferral was honoured. The carrying-cost citation is inverted - that law judges code by maintenance cost and forbids sunk cost steering the next decision, so it argues FOR the refactor, not for postponing it.
guidance_note: When a function's positional parameter list grows past a handful, convert it to an options object in the change that would add the next parameter rather than appending one more.

evidence: Two go.mod files bumping the same module produce a joined list that repeats the path, while the directive says 'For EACH of these bumped modules ... exactly ONCE' - the text and the data disagree, and `[...new Set(...)]` makes the instruction true of what is rendered.
guidance_note: When rendering a list into an instruction that says 'each ... exactly once', de-duplicate at the render site so the instruction is literally true of the text produced.

evidence: I checked the machine: `command -v lit` resolves to a local Mach-O binary at ~/.local/bin/lit and `lit quickstart` prints subcommand guidance text with no network fetch, so the reviewer's 'download and execute code' premise is false; the residual point (an instruction telling an agent to run a PATH command without telling the user) is generic. The block also came from the owner's pre-existing chore commit 517f395 riding in the branch.
guidance_note: Keep an unrelated owner-authored chore commit off a feature branch - it puts files the PR does not own in front of the reviewer and buys threads the PR cannot act on.

evidence: Identical claim to F7 against CLAUDE.md rather than AGENTS.md, and the same check settles it: `lit quickstart` is a local binary printing guidance, not a remote-code fetch. The agent posted the same reply verbatim on both threads, so the reviewer's file-splitting cost two threads for one issue.
guidance_note: Keep an unrelated owner-authored chore commit off a feature branch - it puts files the PR does not own in front of the reviewer and buys threads the PR cannot act on.

evidence: The PR adds a third collector tool and the agent updated the sibling statements at lines 15 and 76 but left line 73's hard count 'the two collector tools' wrong; dropping the count rather than incrementing it is the stronger fix and the reviewer offered it.
guidance_note: When a change makes a hard count in prose wrong, grep the document for every restatement of that count and prefer deleting the number over updating it.

evidence: F3's fix (8b1d64d) removed the `|| []`, turning 'adapters return assessments' from a soft assumption into a hard crash-on-violation contract, and did not state that contract anywhere; the agent's own reply found the cli.js factory header still documented the stale shape `-> {summary, findings, usage}`, omitting both scopes and assessments.
guidance_note: When a fix removes a fallback and turns a soft field into a hard contract, update the documented shape at the producing seam in the same commit.

evidence: The reviewer retracted the finding inside its own text ('The concern was unfounded'), and the retraction is right: the assertion `/VERBATIM: github\.com\/a\/b\./` needs a literal period immediately after the path, which a duplicated list ('...a/b, github.com/a/b.') does not provide at that position. The test only exists because F6's fix in 8b1d64d added it (that commit touches test/multiscope.test.js), so the thread is a round cost created by reviewing a fix's new test.

The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive: `gh api commits/ffd1b91` shows it touched only src/engine/cli.js and dist/index.js, not CLAUDE.md. The omission of dependency-diff.js from the module map is real and predates the PR, which extends that module substantially.
guidance_note: When a change substantially extends a module, check the repo's module map names it before opening the PR.

evidence: Flag is a false positive - ffd1b91 touched only src/engine/cli.js, not dependency-diff.js; and the unassessed branch already used UNRESOLVED_GLYPH in the round-0 hunk quoted under F1, so the glyph collision is original-PR logic that the escaping fixes merely re-touched. The collision itself is real: two tally buckets rendered with one token.
guidance_note: Give each distinct state its own presentation token when you introduce the states - one glyph across two tally buckets is a representation collision, not shorthand.

evidence: Verified cd02a2b: F1's fix added escapeHtml plus URL and link-text hardening, but the same untrusted values are emitted as markdown running text inside the <details> body, where `[x](url)` and `**` still fire - the agent's own F1 plan said 'escape must match the rendering context' and then covered only two of the three contexts.
guidance_note: When escaping untrusted text for a sink, enumerate every grammar the sink parses (HTML structure, markdown inline, URL, link text) and cover all of them in the first fix.

evidence: The ffd1b91 flag is a false positive (that commit touched only cli.js), but the gap is the sibling of F2's: on F2 the agent wrote 'my unit tests covered the pieces but not this worker-to-aggregation seam' and added exactly one seam test, leaving the buildPrMaterial-to-buildReviewInput closure of the same feature untested - swapping its 7th and 8th args would still have passed.
guidance_note: When a missed seam test is found, enumerate every other seam the same feature threads through and cover them in the same commit rather than the one the reviewer named.

narrative: A feature PR that shipped one genuine feature-breaking bug (F2, assessments dropped at the worker seam) and one real security defect (F1, HTML injection into the posted review body), both caught in round 0. Three of the five rounds were driven by findings the agent's own fixes created or failed to sweep: F3's fallback removal created the undocumented adapter contract F10 raised, and F1's HTML-only escaping left the markdown-injection half that F14 raised a round later. Two rounds were also spent on an owner-authored lit chore commit riding in the branch (F7/F8), which the agent correctly pushed back on after actually running the command. The reviewer emitted one self-retracting finding (F11) on a test that an earlier fix had just added.
guidance_observations: A fix that removes a fallback should carry the contract documentation the removal now requires, in the same commit.
Escaping fixes should be scoped by sink grammar, not by the vector the reviewer happened to name - F1 and F14 are one defect paid for twice.
Unrelated chore commits riding in a feature branch produce findings the PR cannot act on and cost a full reply cycle each.
The reviewer posted a finding it retracted inside its own body; the review prompt should drop a finding whose own text withdraws it rather than spending a thread on it.

evidence: listReviewComments returns every inline comment on the PR, so top-level-vs-reply cannot separate RA from a human reviewer, and the code comment explicitly claimed 'no author-identity lookup ... is needed'; the agent accepted that but filtered by `pull_request_review_id` membership in the marker-bearing review set rather than the proposed bot-login compare, which reuses the one REVIEW_MARKER gate and survives a custom GITHUB_REVIEW_TOKEN identity.
guidance_note: Before writing a comment asserting that structure alone identifies a party, check what the API returns for the whole resource - the assumption held only for the subset the author had in mind.

evidence: Same defect as F1 stated in single-enforcer terms, with the exact fix the agent adopted: summarizePriorReviews already identified RA reviews by REVIEW_MARKER, and pairPushbacks re-decided the question structurally instead of consuming that gate's output.
guidance_note: Derive an 'is this ours' predicate from the marker gate that already exists rather than re-deciding it structurally at each new consumer.

evidence: `in_reply_to_id` separates reply from non-reply, never author from bystander, while the prompt block asserts 'the author replied'; the agent chose to make the filter prove the claim rather than take the reviewer's alternative of weakening the prompt wording, which is the stronger of the two options offered.
guidance_note: When prompt text asserts who authored something, make the producing filter prove that claim at the time you write the text.

evidence: The fetch is additive context for the reviewer prompt, so an API blip aborting a paid review is the wrong failure mode; the agent implemented the reviewer's conclusion in 6cedac9 despite the lexical reply-hint reading as pushback.
guidance_note: Classify each pre-review fetch as gating or additive as you add it, and give the additive ones a warn-and-degrade path in the same commit.

evidence: The reviewer's factual half is right and important - the code comment claimed the other pre-review fetches bare-propagate when they in fact catch locally and setFailed with PR context - but its prescription (setFailed + return) contradicts the sibling finding F4 on the same line; the agent took the descriptive-message point and rejected the abort, splitting the answer correctly.
guidance_note: When a comment asserts how sibling call sites behave, read those call sites before writing it - the false claim is what drew two contradictory findings onto one line.

evidence: Both the `c.user?.login !== authorLogin` filter and the comment claiming 'authorLogin absent ... matches nothing' arrived in 7ececee, F3's fix; with authorLogin undefined and a ghost-user reply, `undefined !== undefined` is false and the reply passes, so the fix shipped a comment its own code did not enforce.
guidance_note: When a fix adds a filter plus a comment stating its degradation invariant, enforce the invariant once as a precondition rather than asserting it about the filter's incidental behaviour.

evidence: The reviewer states inside the finding that the missing field is benign because pairPushbacks never reads a reply's pull_request_review_id, so there is no defect - only a readability request, which the agent satisfied with a one-line fixture comment. The fixture's findingReviewIds shape exists only because F2's fix introduced review-id filtering.
guidance_note: When a fix adds a test fixture that deliberately omits a field the production code ignores, annotate the omission in the fixture as you write it.

evidence: The reviewer supplies an exact falsifier - dropping priorPushbacks from the buildWorkerPrompt closure at multiscope.js:295 leaves every test in the file green - and the existing tests call buildReviewInput directly, bypassing the closure. The threading is original-PR code; no earlier fix in this PR touched multiscope.js.
guidance_note: For every value threaded through a closure, write the test that fails when the argument is dropped - exercising the endpoint function directly never covers the closure.

evidence: I checked this PR's own comments via the API: replies 3695343059 and 3695347390 both carry in_reply_to_id 3695339943, the thread root, not each other - GitHub flattens review-comment threads, so the nested chain the reviewer describes cannot occur and repliesByParent.get(finding.id) is complete. The agent verified the same way and documented the invariant instead of adding a traversal.
guidance_note: Document the platform invariant a structural assumption rests on at the point you rely on it, so a reviewer does not have to infer it from behaviour.

narrative: Round 0 produced three findings that are really one defect - pairPushbacks distinguished roles structurally when listReviewComments returns every comment on the PR - and the agent's single fix (identity on both sides, sourced from the existing REVIEW_MARKER gate) was better than the bot-login compare the reviewer proposed. That fix then cost round 2: it introduced both the ghost-user corner (F6) and the ambiguous test fixture (F7). Round 1 put two contradictory prescriptions on one line (F4 wants degrade, F5 wants abort); the agent reconciled them on an essential-versus-additive split, which is the right call. The only pushback of substance, F9, was correct and I confirmed it independently against the API.
guidance_observations: Three round-0 findings restating one defect suggest the reviewer's per-scope workers duplicate rather than dedupe when several scopes see the same function.
A single round can carry mutually exclusive prescriptions on one line; the address-pr-reviews loop handled it well by answering the shared premise once and splitting the fix.
A fix that adds both a filter and a comment about its degradation should enforce the comment's claim, or the next round finds the gap between them.
A false claim in a code comment about sibling call sites drew two findings by itself - comment accuracy is a review-round cost, not just documentation hygiene.

evidence: The exclude-patterns default string is byte-identical in freeze-case.sh, action.yml:70, README.md:95 and code-review.yml:45, and the frozen cases record the value the script used - so a drift silently produces cases replaying under conditions the action no longer has; the agent made action.yml the source and aborts loudly if the read fails.
guidance_note: When a script needs a default that a manifest already declares, read it from the manifest and abort loudly on a failed read - a 'keep in sync' comment is not a source of truth.

evidence: The README asserted the diffHunk substring property was 'verified at freeze time' while freeze-case.sh copied .diff_hunk straight from the API with no check; the agent took the reviewer's option (a) and made the sentence true by construction for every future case rather than rewording it away.
guidance_note: When documentation says an invariant is verified by a script, the verification goes into that script in the same commit as the sentence.

narrative: Two accurate advisory findings in round 0, both accepted and fixed correctly, and round 1 came back clean - the shortest and cleanest PR in the batch. Both findings were about a claim in text (a duplicated constant, a documented-but-absent verification) rather than about executing code, and in both cases the agent chose the fix that makes the claim true by construction over the fix that weakens the claim. Nothing here was fix-caused.
guidance_observations: Both findings were 'the text claims something the code does not do' - a pre-push self-check for that class would have caught them without a round.
Choosing the option that makes the documented claim true, rather than rewording the claim, is the pattern that kept this PR at two rounds.

evidence: parseInt('2.5', 10) is 2 and the surrounding check tested only isNaN and < 1, so the accept set did not match the error message's promise of a positive integer - for a harness whose baseline depends on the exact repeat count that is a silent lie; eeae81a's parsePositiveInt uses Number + Number.isInteger.
guidance_note: Make the accept set match the error message - Number() plus Number.isInteger, never parseInt, when the message promises 'positive integer'.

evidence: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive: eeae81a's patch touches only parseArgs and the new parsePositiveInt helper, while the unconsumed excludePatterns field is original-PR code. The defect is real - production calls filterFiles before buildPrMaterial and the runner did not, so a replay of a raw three-dot diff would review a superset of the original file set; c427040 inserts production's own filterFiles seam at the same position.
guidance_note: When a harness replays a production pipeline, walk production's ordered steps and reuse each seam - a manifest field nothing reads is the signal a step was skipped.

evidence: The reviewer names the cause itself: '-n and --workers are protected by parsePositiveInt ... but --out has no such guard' - F1's fix hardened two of the three flags the same assignment loop feeds and left the third. The agent's variant is better than the proposed one: I read 051445c and the guard keys on '--' so that `--workers -1` still reaches parsePositiveInt for the accurate message.
guidance_note: When hardening one flag's value in a hand-rolled argument parser, cover every flag that same assignment loop feeds in the same commit.

evidence: The 051445c flag is a false positive - that commit is a six-line guard inside parseArgs and does not touch parseCaseManifest, which is original-PR code. The defect is real: manifest.name is required only to be a non-empty string and then flows into path.join, so '../../../tmp/evil' escapes eval/out entirely.
guidance_note: A string used as a path component must be parsed as one at its boundary (name === path.basename(name)), not merely required non-empty.

evidence: Same false-positive flag as F4 (051445c touched only parseArgs). The gap is real and mechanical: parseCaseManifest applies its own `req` non-empty helper to provider and model but checks reasoning with typeof alone, so '' survives parse and resurfaces downstream as a confusing 'Reasoning-pin mismatch'.
guidance_note: When a parser has a `req` helper for its string fields, route every string field through it - the one field checked by typeof alone is where the gap will be.

narrative: Five rounds on a 519-line PR, and every round after the first raised a boundary-validation gap in the same two parse functions the previous round had already been reading. Only one round is strictly fix-caused: F1 hardened two of the three flags in parseArgs and F3 came back a round later for the third. The rest is under-sweeping in the original PR - F4 and F5 are two untouched gaps in one parseCaseManifest, raised together only because the reviewer happened to find them in the same pass. Every ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag in this packet is a false positive; each named fix commit is a tightly scoped patch to a function the next finding does not touch. The agent's fixes were consistently accurate and in two cases better-reasoned than the proposal.
guidance_observations: The reviewer discovers one boundary gap per round in the same function instead of sweeping the parse layer once - a per-round finding budget is not the constraint; scope coverage is.
After the first parse-boundary finding, the agent should have swept every parser in the file and offered the sweep in the reply; that alone collapses rounds 2 through 4.
The agent's guard-on-'--'-not-'-' reasoning on F3 avoided a regression the reviewer's literal fix would have caused - explaining the deviation in the plan is what made that reviewable.

evidence: loadCache returned whatever parseJson produced, and makeLlmJudge then evaluates `ck in cache` - a number or string on disk parses fine and breaks inland with a TypeError naming neither the cache nor the file; ecf8ffe adds the plain-object assert with the delete-and-rebuild message.
guidance_note: When a parse boundary yields JSON that downstream code indexes as a map, prove the object type at the boundary and sweep every sibling parser in the file in the same pass.

evidence: The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is a false positive: ecf8ffe's patch touches only loadCache and the module exports, while callJudge is original-PR code round 0 did not flag. The claim is accurate and modestly scoped - the reviewer itself notes the failure is already loud and only the diagnosis is obscure - and every other arm of callJudge already names the judge in its error, so the wrap is consistency, not defence.
guidance_note: When every other arm of an I/O function names itself in its error message, wrap the remaining throwing call the same way as you write the function.

evidence: Verified ecf8ffe changed loadCache alone; parseUsage and parseMeta carried the identical unproven-object boundary from the original PR and the reviewer cites loadCache's fix as the precedent it did not sweep to. The agent accepted but replaced the reviewer's per-parser assert with one parseJsonObject(raw, label) that expected.json, usage.json, meta.json and the cache all route through, folding the ecf8ffe copy in - a better fix than the one proposed.
guidance_note: When a boundary-validation gap is found in one parser, sweep every sibling parser in the file and factor the check once, rather than patching only the instance named.

evidence: The parseMeta half of the same un-swept gap: meta.json containing the literal `null` crashes at typeof null.case. Flagged against 4b1e0b1, whose patch touches only callJudge, so the flag is a false positive - the real cause is F1's single-instance fix. One shared reply and one shared fix (c68f23c's parseJsonObject) closed F3 and F4 together.
guidance_note: When a reviewer cites an earlier fix as precedent for a new finding, read that as evidence the earlier fix under-swept and fix the whole class in one commit.

narrative: Round 0 found one real parse-boundary gap in loadCache; the agent fixed exactly that instance, and round 2 came back with the same gap in parseUsage and parseMeta, explicitly citing the loadCache fix as the precedent. That is one wholly avoidable round, and the agent's eventual response was the right shape - factoring a single parseJsonObject enforcer that all four object parsers route through, collapsing the earlier inline copy. Round 1's finding (F2, judge-response error context) is unrelated to the loadCache fix despite the ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag and is diagnostics polish rather than a defect. All three ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flags in this packet are false positives; the fix commits are small and land in functions the next round's findings do not touch.
guidance_observations: The clearest avoidable round in the batch: fixing the named instance instead of the class cost exactly one round, and the agent knew the class - it factored the shared enforcer the moment it was asked twice.
The reply-hint on F2 read as pushback while the reply opened 'Plan: Valid' - the lexical hint is unreliable on this repo's replies and should not be used for triage.
The reviewer's round-2 findings named the earlier fix as precedent; that phrasing is a reliable signal for the address-pr-reviews loop that a class, not an instance, is in play.
